mcqs.question: Two separate NSManagedObjectContexts fetch the same underlying row and each make different uncommitted edits. What's true before either context saves?
options: Both contexts hold independent, potentially conflicting versions of that entity in memory until one saves
Core Data automatically merges the two contexts' changes in real time
The second context to fetch is blocked until the first context saves or rolls back
This is not possible — Core Data enforces a single context per entity instance
mcqs.explanation: A context is a staging area, not the source of truth; two contexts can independently hold different uncommitted versions of the same underlying data until a save reconciles with the store, which is exactly why passing objects across contexts naively causes subtle bugs. There's no automatic real-time merge or fetch-blocking behavior.

mcqs.question: A fetch request filters on isComplete == NO using an NSPredicate. Where does that filtering actually happen for the default SQLite-backed store?
options: In Swift, after Core Data loads every row of the entity into memory
On a background thread that scans the whole table regardless of the predicate
In the UI layer, after the fetch request returns unfiltered results
At the store level, translated into a SQL WHERE clause, so unmatched rows are never loaded into memory
mcqs.explanation: NSPredicate on a fetch request is translated down to the store level — SQL for the default SQLite store — so filtering happens before rows are materialized into memory, which is what lets it scale. Filtering in Swift after loading everything would defeat the point of using a predicate at all.

mcqs.question: A new app targets iOS 17+ only, needs an object graph with relationships, and the team wants strong compile-time query checking. Which is the strongest default choice?
options: A plain SQLite wrapper, since it gives full query control
Core Data, since it's more mature than SwiftData
SwiftData, since it offers the same object-graph model with type-safe #Predicate queries and less boilerplate, and the OS floor supports it
Neither — object graphs should always be avoided in favor of flat key-value storage
mcqs.explanation: With no need to support pre-iOS-17 devices, SwiftData's type-safe predicates and lower boilerplate make it the stronger default while still providing the object-graph capability Core Data offers underneath. A plain SQLite wrapper gives up the object-graph and type-safety benefits the team explicitly wants.

mcqs.question: A new app version splits one entity into two related entities to better model the data. What kind of migration does this require?
options: Lightweight migration, since Core Data can always infer any structural change automatically
No migration is needed if the app is reinstalled by the user
Custom (heavyweight) migration, since splitting an entity isn't a structurally inferable change lightweight migration handles
This change is not possible without deleting all existing user data
mcqs.explanation: Lightweight migration only covers structurally inferable changes like adding an optional property or a simple rename; splitting one entity into two requires a custom mapping model or migration policy code, since Core Data can't infer how existing rows should be divided between the new entities on its own.

mcqs.question: A managed object fetched on the main context is passed directly to a background queue closure that reads one of its properties. What's the risk?
options: No risk — NSManagedObject is thread-safe for read access from any queue
A real, reproducible crash or data corruption, since managed objects and their context aren't safe to access outside that context's own queue
The property read will simply return nil instead of crashing
The risk only applies to write access, never to reads
mcqs.explanation: Managed objects are tied to their context's queue for all access, reads included — touching one from an arbitrary background thread is a real crash risk or silent corruption, not just a write-only concern. The safe pattern is context.perform{} or passing a thread-safe NSManagedObjectID and re-fetching on the target context.

mcqs.question: A fetch request with no fetchBatchSize or fetchLimit runs against a table that has grown to 50,000 rows in production. What's the practical consequence?
options: Core Data automatically caps results at 1,000 rows regardless of configuration
The whole result set materializes into memory at once, risking a memory spike and UI stall that didn't show up when testing against a small seed dataset
The fetch silently fails and returns an empty array
Performance is unaffected since Core Data always streams results lazily by default
mcqs.explanation: Without fetchBatchSize, Core Data materializes the full result set rather than streaming it in chunks, so a query that felt instant against a hundred seed rows in testing can cause a real memory and performance problem once production data grows — exactly the kind of bug that doesn't surface until scale. There's no automatic 1,000-row cap and no silent-failure behavior here.
